Title: California Law Will Require AI Developers to Disclose Training Data | PYMNTS.com

Summary: 
California’s Assembly Bill 2013, the Generative Artificial Intelligence Training Data Transparency Act, signed in 2024, will take effect at the start of 2026. The law requires AI developers to publish on their websites detailed information about the datasets that train their models, including sources, whether the data are publicly available or proprietary, size and type, whether copyrighted or personal data are included, and the time period during which the data were collected. Bloomberg Law described AB 2013 as one of the most comprehensive U.S. rules on AI disclosure, noting that compliance will not be simple. Goodwin Law explained that implementing AB 2013 presents several key challenges for developers of generative AI systems. One of the foremost difficulties lies in assembling comprehensive documentation of training datasets, especially for models that have evolved over time. Many generative models incorporate data from heterogeneous sources, some of which may lack clear provenance or licensing information. The disclosure mandate could help trace which datasets were used in lawsuits alleging models were trained on copyrighted works without permission, and could provide a foundation for independent audits and risk assessments. Business‑tech executives warned the bill could have a "chilling effect" on development in California, with startups particularly exposed to compliance burdens, according to The Wall Street Journal. Conversely, Microsoft’s Chief Scientist Eric Horvitz said that oversight, if "done properly," can accelerate advances in AI by encouraging more responsible data use and building public trust in new systems. California has historically shaped national tech regulation; if the disclosure requirements prove workable, other states could follow, giving the law significance beyond California’s borders. Colorado has delayed its AI act implementation to June 2026, illustrating the broader policy debate over whether transparency alone will be enough. The law signals that disclosure may soon become a baseline expectation across industries, as noted by PYMNTS when Citi unveiled its upgraded platform.

Title: California becomes first US state to require AI transparency

Summary: 
California has become the first U.S. state to enact an AI transparency law, signing Senate Bill 53 (the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act) into law on September 30, 2025. The law mandates that large AI developers—defined as firms with annual gross revenue exceeding $500 million and those training frontier models using more than 10²⁶ operations—must publish and update AI frameworks, file incident reports with the state Office of Emergency Services, and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers. Critical safety incidents include unauthorized model access causing death or injury, catastrophic risks (defined as harm to over 50 people or $1 billion in property damage), loss of control of a frontier model, or a model deceiving its developers to bypass restrictions. The law marks a shift from SB 1047, which Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed a year earlier due to its narrow focus on only the largest models, creating a false sense of security. Newsom convened a working group that helped shape SB 53, which now emphasizes a 'show your work' compliance model over a 'do no harm' mandate. Critics, including the Chamber of Progress (representing Amazon, Google, and NVIDIA), argue the law imposes a 'compliance minefield' with penalties tied to paperwork failures rather than actual harm, and that the 10²⁶ FLOPS threshold is an arbitrary proxy for risk. Despite criticism, proponents like Anthropic's Jack Clark praise SB 53 for establishing meaningful transparency without prescriptive technical rules. A key bipartisan agreement is the creation of 'CalCompute,' a publicly accessible computing cluster led by the Government Operations Agency (GOA), intended to democratize AI development by providing equitable access to critical infrastructure. CalCompute’s implementation timeline is extended, with the GOA required to submit a report on its setup by early 2027. The law’s provisions take effect on January 1, 2026.

Title: California law mandates increased developer transparency for large AI models

Summary: 
California Governor Gavin Newsom signed the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (TFAIA), also known as SB 53, into law on September 29, 2025. The law, effective January 1, 2026, imposes broad transparency and reporting requirements on developers of 'frontier models'—AI models trained using more than 10^26 FLOPs, a threshold higher than the EU AI Act's 10^25 FLOPs. 'Large frontier developers'—those with annual gross revenues exceeding $500 million—are subject to stricter obligations. These include publishing a 'frontier AI framework' detailing technical and organizational protocols for managing catastrophic risks, updating it annually or within 30 days of a 'material modification' (undefined), and releasing a 'transparency report' before deploying new or substantially modified frontier models. The report must include the model's release date, supported languages and modalities, intended uses, and usage restrictions. Large frontier developers must also include summaries of risk assessments and third-party involvement. Developers must report 'critical safety incidents' to the Office of Emergency Services (OES) within 15 days (or 24 hours if imminent harm is involved), with OES required to publish anonymized annual reports starting in 2027. The law prohibits materially false or misleading statements about catastrophic risks or the frontier AI framework and includes whistleblower protections for employees with reasonable cause to report dangers or violations. The Attorney General may impose civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation. A state consortium within the Government Operations Agency will develop a framework for CalCompute, a public cloud computing cluster for safe, ethical, and sustainable AI research, with a report due January 1, 2027. The law applies to 'large frontier developers'—those with annual revenue exceeding $500 million—and specifically targets frontier AI models trained on more than 10^26 FLOPs, a threshold higher than the EU AI Act’s 10^25 FLOPs. Developers must also issue transparency reports upon releasing or substantially modifying a model, including intended uses, modalities, and results of catastrophic-risk assessments. Title: How text and data drive the future of copyright in AI

Summary: 
The article discusses how generative AI’s reliance on large datasets—much of it sourced from the web, proprietary collections, and licensed materials—creates significant intellectual‑property concerns. It notes that major AI firms are embroiled in worldwide litigation, often as class actions, over alleged copyright infringement. In 2024, authors Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber and Kirk Wallace Johnson sued Anthropic, claiming the company trained its Claude models on millions of books, including theirs, without permission or compensation. In June 2025, the U.S. Court of the Northern District of California ruled that Anthropic’s use of legally acquired books fell under fair use because the training process did not simply reproduce the originals but generated new content after learning statistical patterns; however, the court found that building a central library from downloaded pirated copies was not fair use, potentially exposing Anthropic to substantial damages in a forthcoming trial expected later in 2025. The case is certified as a class action, meaning U.S. authors whose works were allegedly used from pirated sources could be represented, which could have serious financial implications for Anthropic as it prepares to close a new $5 billion funding round that would value the company at about $170 billion.

In India, the Delhi High Court is hearing a major copyright case filed by news agency ANI against U.S.‑based OpenAI. The court’s decision is expected to clarify whether the use of copyrighted material in training large language models constitutes infringement under Indian law, which relies on the principle of fair dealing under Section 52 of the Copyright Act 1957. The Indian law lists more than 30 scenarios where use of protected material does not amount to infringement, but it does not explicitly mention training data for AI. The article argues that India’s common‑law framework allows courts to interpret the law in light of technological advances, presenting an opportunity for policymakers to amend copyright law to create an exception for computational data analysis and processing without prior approval from copyright owners.

Summary: 
Google's Gmail has come under scrutiny for potentially using user emails and Workspace content to train its AI models, despite claims in its End User License Agreements (EULAs) that such data would not be used without explicit consent. In 2023, Google expanded these features with AI capabilities like automated writing, reminders, and enhanced email sorting, integrating them under the same Smart Features umbrella without requesting new consent. A 2025 update, referenced in a lawsuit by PolitiFact, further fueled confusion: Google states it will not use private messages, searches, or Drive files to train language models only if Smart Features are disabled. However, many users unknowingly left these features enabled since 2013, creating a legal gray area. This ambiguity has led to a class-action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, alleging Google used private data from Smart Features to train Bard and Gemini without proper transparency. Media outlets like Forbes and users such as Dave Jones (@eevblog) have highlighted this loophole and provided instructions to disable AI training by turning off Smart Features in Gmail settings. Disabling these features means losing automated email categorization (e.g., Promotions, Social tabs), though emails still go to their respective folders—users must now access them via the left sidebar. Other Google services like Drive and Calendar retain data but lose AI-powered reminders. The controversy raises concerns about informed consent and could lead to future legal or regulatory consequences, especially given Google’s recent antitrust lawsuits and a €2.9 billion fine for abusive practices.

TFAIA defines 'catastrophic risks' as foreseeable threats that could cause death or serious injury to over 50 people or over $1 billion in property damage through activities like weapon development, autonomous cyberattacks, or evasion of control. The law includes strong whistleblower protections, prohibiting retaliation against employees who report safety concerns and requiring large developers to provide anonymous reporting mechanisms. Violations by large frontier developers can result in civil penalties of up to $1 million per incident, enforced by the California Attorney General. TFAIA includes a safe harbor provision, deeming compliance with federal standards deemed 'substantially equivalent to or stricter than' TFAIA as sufficient. The legislation follows the veto of a broader 2024 bill (SB 1047) and precedes the New York legislature’s passage of the RAISE Act, which differs in defining frontier models by training cost ($100M+) and includes pre-deployment safeguards and prohibitions on high-risk deployments, but lacks whistleblower protections. Governor Newsom emphasized TFAIA as a 'blueprint' for national AI policy and a compliance pathway aligned with future federal standards.

articles.title: How text and data drive the future of copyright in AI
articles.summary:
The article discusses how generative AI’s reliance on large datasets—much of it sourced from the web, proprietary collections, and licensed materials—creates significant intellectual‑property concerns. It notes that major AI firms are embroiled in worldwide litigation, often as class actions, over alleged copyright infringement. In 2024, authors Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber and Kirk Wallace Johnson sued Anthropic, claiming the company trained its Claude models on millions of books, including theirs, without permission or compensation. In June 2025, the U.S. Court of the Northern District of California ruled that Anthropic’s use of legally acquired books fell under fair use because the training process did not simply reproduce the originals but generated new content after learning statistical patterns; however, the court found that building a central library from downloaded pirated copies was not fair use, potentially exposing Anthropic to substantial damages in a forthcoming trial expected later in 2025. The case is certified as a class action, meaning U.S. authors whose works were allegedly used from pirated sources could be represented, which could have serious financial implications for Anthropic as it prepares to close a new $5 billion funding round that would value the company at about $170 billion.

In India, the Delhi High Court is hearing a major copyright case filed by news agency ANI against U.S.‑based OpenAI. The court’s decision is expected to clarify whether the use of copyrighted material in training large language models constitutes infringement under Indian law, which relies on the principle of fair dealing under Section 52 of the Copyright Act 1957. The Indian law lists more than 30 scenarios where use of protected material does not amount to infringement, but it does not explicitly mention training data for AI. The article argues that India’s common‑law framework allows courts to interpret the law in light of technological advances, presenting an opportunity for policymakers to amend copyright law to create an exception for computational data analysis and processing without prior approval from copyright owners.

Key metrics: 2024 lawsuit by Bartz, Graeber and Johnson; 2025 U.S. court ruling; potential damages in a 2025 trial; $5 billion funding round; $170 billion valuation; India’s Section 52 fair dealing provision.

Quotes from the article: 'the AI training process did not simply reproduce the original works, but generated new content after learning statistical patterns.'

articles.title: Google Faces Scrutiny Over Gmail AI Training Practices Amid Consent and Legal Ambiguity
articles.summary: Google's Gmail has come under scrutiny for potentially using user emails and Workspace content to train its AI models, despite claims in its End User License Agreements (EULAs) that such data would not be used without explicit consent. The issue stems from a 2013 update that introduced 'Smart Features' in Gmail, which required user consent at the time but did not mention AI or language models—concepts that did not exist then. In 2023, Google expanded these features with AI capabilities like automated writing, reminders, and enhanced email sorting, integrating them under the same Smart Features umbrella without requesting new consent. A 2025 update, referenced in a lawsuit by PolitiFact, further fueled confusion: Google states it will not use private messages, searches, or Drive files to train language models only if Smart Features are disabled. However, many users unknowingly left these features enabled since 2013, creating a legal gray area. This ambiguity has led to a class-action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, alleging Google used private data from Smart Features to train Bard and Gemini without proper transparency. Media outlets like Forbes and users such as Dave Jones (@eevblog) have highlighted this loophole and provided instructions to disable AI training by turning off Smart Features in Gmail settings. Disabling these features means losing automated email categorization (e.g., Promotions, Social tabs), though emails still go to their respective folders—users must now access them via the left sidebar. Other Google services like Drive and Calendar retain data but lose AI-powered reminders. The controversy raises concerns about informed consent and could lead to future legal or regulatory consequences, especially given Google’s recent antitrust lawsuits and a €2.9 billion fine for abusive practices.
